title: Flynn's taxonomy
info: Classifies computer architectures by number of instruction streams × number of data streams: SISD, SIMD, MISD, MIMD.

title: SISD
info: Single instruction stream, single data stream. A simple sequential computer.

title: SIMD
info: Single instruction stream, multiple data streams. Vector or array computers.
example: A GPU applies the same shading instruction to millions of pixels at once.

title: MISD
info: Multiple instruction streams, single data stream. Fault-tolerant systems that compute redundantly on the same data and vote.
example: The Space Shuttle's four flight computers voting on every output.

title: MIMD
info: Multiple instruction streams, multiple data streams. Multi-core processors, distributed systems and networks.
example: An 8-core laptop running Chrome, Spotify and Zoom at once.

title: Pipe-and-filter architecture
info: Each component processes ("filters") a message and passes the result to the next component.
example: `cat log | grep 404 | sort`; a compiler's lexer → parser → code generator.

title: Blackboard architecture
info: One central component handles all communication; every component reads from and writes to it instead of talking to each other.
example: A hospital patient chart that the doctor, lab and pharmacy all read and write.

title: Event-driven architecture
info: Events determine the execution flow. Components subscribe to an event source, which notifies them, and they handle the event in a callback.
example: Any GUI: nothing happens until you click or type.

title: Characteristics of distributed systems
info: Resource sharing and synchronization; openness and standards; concurrency and parallelism; scalability; dependability and fault tolerance; transparency.

title: Transparency (distributed systems)
info: Users can't see where or how a resource is located, replicated or moved; the system looks like one machine.
example: You don't know which Google server holds your Doc.

title: Issues of distributed vs. centralized systems
info: More complexity; communication and connectivity problems; security and reliability risks; unpredictable, non-deterministic behavior.

title: Two-tier (client-server) architecture
info: Servers provide services and clients use them. Clients know the servers, but servers don't need to know the clients. Clients and servers are logical processes, so they can share a machine, and the mapping needn't be one-to-one.

title: Thin client
info: The server does all processing and data management; the client only runs the GUI.
example: Remote Desktop or Citrix.

title: Fat (thick) client
info: The client runs the application logic and UI; the server only manages data.
example: Desktop Excel with OneDrive; video games; HTML5 apps.

title: Three-tier architecture
info: Presentation tier, application-processing tier and data-management tier. Balances performance better than thin client, is simpler to manage than fat client, and scales by adding servers.
example: Online banking; Canvas.

title: Four-tier architecture with a service layer
info: The application is composed mostly from existing services in a service repository. An example of SOA (though SOA need not be tiered).

title: Eight fallacies of distributed computing
info: False assumptions: the network is reliable; latency is zero; bandwidth is infinite; the network is secure; topology doesn't change; there is one administrator; transport cost is zero; the network is homogeneous.

title: Distributed object architecture
info: No distinction between clients and servers: any object can provide services to others and use theirs. Objects communicate through an ORB (software bus).

title: Pros and cons of distributed object architecture
info: Pros: open, flexible, scalable, can reconfigure dynamically, lets designers delay where services live. Cons: harder to design than client-server, no separation of duties, competing standards.

title: ORB (Object Request Broker)
info: Middleware ("software bus") that handles communication between distributed objects. The caller binds to an IDL stub; the ORB calls the target object through its IDL skeleton.

title: IDL stub
info: The client-side stand-in generated from an IDL interface. Calling the stub sends the call through the ORB to the remote object.

title: CORBA
info: The Object Management Group (OMG) standard for an ORB. Interfaces are written in IDL and mapped to many languages, so objects in different languages interoperate.

title: DCOM
info: Microsoft's competing distributed object approach (OLE → COM → COM+ → DCOM), later folded into .NET.

title: ESB (Enterprise Service Bus)
info: The service-oriented version of the ORB. Built on enterprise messaging and loosely coupled, unlike classic tightly coupled EAI.
example: 8 systems wired pairwise need 8×7/2 = 28 links; with an ESB, 8.

title: Design pattern
info: A reusable, general template for solving a recurring design problem. It is not a finished design, and algorithms are not design patterns.

title: Singleton pattern
info: Creational. Guarantees exactly one instance of a class, with a global access point.
example: An app's single shared logger.

title: Factory method pattern
info: Creational. A creation method (or subclass) decides which concrete class to instantiate.
example: .NET's `XmlReader.Create(...)`.

title: Abstract factory pattern
info: Creational. Creates families of related objects without naming their concrete classes.
example: A UI kit producing matching Windows-style or Mac-style widgets.

title: Lazy initialization pattern
info: Creational. Delays creating an expensive object until it's first needed.
example: Loading a photo only when you scroll to it.

title: Object pool pattern
info: Creational. Recycles expensive objects instead of creating new ones.
example: A database connection pool; the .NET thread pool.

title: Utility pattern
info: A class with a private constructor and only static methods.
example: `Math.Sqrt(9)`; you never create a Math object.

title: Adapter pattern
info: Structural. Converts one interface into the interface a client expects.
example: A travel plug adapter; wrapping old COBOL code behind a web service.

title: Decorator pattern
info: Structural. Adds responsibilities to an object dynamically, without subclassing.
example: Java's `new BufferedReader(new FileReader(f))`.

title: Façade pattern
info: Structural. One simple interface in front of a complex subsystem.
example: One `PlaceOrder()` call hiding inventory, payment and shipping.

title: Proxy pattern
info: Structural. A surrogate or placeholder that controls access to another object.
example: A web service client proxy; a debit card standing in for your bank account.

title: Command pattern
info: Behavioral. Wraps a request as an object so it can be queued, logged or undone.
example: Undo/redo in Word.

title: Iterator pattern
info: Behavioral. Walks through a collection without exposing its internal structure.
example: C#'s `foreach`.

title: Mediator pattern
info: Behavioral. Objects communicate through a middleman instead of directly with each other.
example: An airport control tower.

title: State pattern
info: Behavioral. An object changes its behavior when its internal state changes.
example: A vending machine that acts differently when idle, paid or sold out.

title: Observer pattern
info: Behavioral. One-to-many dependency: when the subject changes, all its dependents are notified automatically.
example: C# events; subscribing to a YouTube channel.

title: Active Object pattern
info: Concurrency. Separates calling a method from executing it, using async invocation plus a scheduler.
example: Clicking Print returns immediately; the spooler thread prints later.

title: Monitor pattern
info: Concurrency. Synchronizes tasks that share a resource so only one uses it at a time.
example: A single-occupancy restroom with a lock.

title: Read-Write Lock pattern
info: Concurrency. Allows concurrent reads but makes writes exclusive.
example: A Wikipedia page read by thousands while one person edits.

title: Reactor pattern
info: Concurrency. Demultiplexes concurrent requests and dispatches them to handlers.
example: IIS's http.sys request queue; Node.js's event loop.

title: Three-party model (SOA)
info: Service provider, service broker and application builder (service requester). Flow: develop → publish → find → bind → call → result.

title: Service provider
info: Develops services (often active objects) in C#, Java, Python, etc., hosts them, and registers/publishes them with a broker.
example: Stripe providing payment processing.

title: Service broker
info: Keeps the registry and repository (directory) of services, with white, yellow and green pages. Providers publish to it; requesters search it.
example: UDDI, ebXML, RapidAPI.

title: Application builder (service requester)
info: Finds services through the broker, binds to them through proxies, invokes them, and composes them into an application with a GUI for end users.

title: Service
info: The interface between producer and consumer: a well-defined, self-contained module that doesn't depend on other functions' context or state. No human UI; a loosely coupled standard API. Add a GUI and it becomes a (web) application.

title: SOA (Service-Oriented Architecture)
info: An architecture pattern: software made of loosely coupled, platform-independent services that communicate through standard interfaces.

title: SOC (Service-Oriented Computing)
info: The computing paradigm underneath SOA, one level deeper, including algorithms and data structures. Often used interchangeably with SOA.

title: SOD (Service-Oriented Development)
info: The whole development cycle built on SOA and SOC, including tools, databases and hosting.

title: Web services (two kinds)
info: Services reachable over the web. SOAP/WSDL services (heavyweight) and RESTful services (lightweight, microservices).

title: Proxy vs. code migration/integration
info: With a proxy, the code stays with the provider: platform-independent, loosely coupled, provider keeps IP and can upgrade without clients rebuilding. Costs: network latency/bandwidth on every call and dependence on the provider being up.
example: A store calling Stripe gets new fraud checks free, but checkout fails if Stripe is down.

title: OOC vs. SOC
info: OOC: classes, inheritance, polymorphism, in-process binding, reuse by integrating code, one team. SOC: loosely coupled platform-independent services, standard interfaces, remote (often dynamic) binding via proxies, message-based, three separate parties.

title: XML
info: A meta-language used to define other languages (SOAP, WSDL, UDDI, BPEL, RDF, OWL). You define your own tags, and every tag must be closed.

title: XML vs. HTML
info: HTML tags are predefined and format data for display; some can be left open. XML tags describe the meaning of data, require a schema, and are easy for machines to interpret.

title: SOAP
info: The protocol that carries messages between services and applications. A SOAP message is an XML document, Envelope → Header + Body, usually inside an HTTP packet.
example: Header = writing on the envelope; Body = the letter; HTTP = the mail truck.

title: MIME
info: Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions. Extends email format to support non-text attachments, multi-part bodies and non-ASCII headers.

title: WSDL (four aspects)
info: Web Services Description Language describes: functionality (in a taxonomy), the contract (parameter and return types), the binding (transport protocol, usually SOAP), and the address (URL). The last three can be generated automatically.

title: WSDL element structure
info: definitions (root) → service → port (URL) → binding (SOAP) → portType → operation → message in/out → types.

title: WSDL ↔ OO mapping
info: WSDL interface ↔ interface; namespace ↔ namespace; service ↔ class; operation ↔ method; input type ↔ parameters; output type ↔ return value. Binding and address have no OO equivalent.

title: Invoking a web service vs. RPC
info: You invoke a web service by sending a message in a standard protocol, not by a remote procedure call: loosely coupled vs. tightly coupled, data flow vs. control flow.

title: [ServiceContract] / [OperationContract]
info: WCF attributes. [ServiceContract] marks the service interface; [OperationContract] marks each method that clients may call remotely. Unmarked methods stay internal.

title: OASIS
info: A nonprofit standards consortium (founded 1993 as SGML Open); the largest standards body for SOA and web services (UDDI, ebXML).

title: UDDI white pages
info: Provider information: business name, identifiers (e.g. DUNS number), contact details. Lookup by name.

title: UDDI yellow pages
info: Categorization: industry, product/service type, location. Lookup by category.

title: UDDI green pages
info: Technical information: the data structures, interfaces and APIs (URLs, protocols) a program needs to use the service.

title: ebXML (five modules)
info: Business Process Specification Schema; Core Components; Collaboration Protocol Profiles and Agreements (CPPA); Message Service; Registry & Repository.

title: Registry vs. repository
info: A registry stores metadata about artifacts (like a library catalog); a repository stores the artifacts themselves (the shelves). ebXML integrates both.

title: Federated ebXML registry / SAML
info: Multiple registries linked to act as one, using SAML for federated identity (single sign-on). Used in healthcare and government.
example: The Government of Canada case linking federal and provincial registries.

title: Kinds of service brokers
info: OASIS UDDI (limited automation; large IT companies), OASIS ebXML (extensive automation; government and non-IT), and ad hoc lists (manual search, e.g. a university's public service list).

title: Web application vs. web service
info: A web application is for end users and has a GUI. A web service is for application builders and has an API (service interface).

title: Service proxy (client side)
info: A "virtual" object that opens a channel to the remote service. It contains each remote method's name, parameter list and return type, but no source code.
example: A TV remote: a button for every function, none of the TV's electronics.

title: Endpoint (ABC)
info: An operation interface a service exposes. Address (where: the URL), Binding (how: protocol, e.g. BasicHttpsBinding), Contract (what: operations, parameter and return types).

title: BasicHttpBinding → BasicHttpsBinding
info: When a service requires HTTPS, its clients change the binding in Web.config from BasicHttpBinding to BasicHttpsBinding.

title: Three levels of SOA application building
info: Architecture/interface specification (SCA, Oracle SOA Suite); process/workflow (BPEL, Windows Workflow Foundation, WSFL, XLANG); code (C#/Java binding through WSDL, SOAP, HTTP).

title: BPEL
info: Business Process Execution Language: an XML workflow language that describes the steps of a process and which service performs each step.
example: An insurance claim: Submitted → Assigned → Approved → Paid.

title: SOA myths vs. facts
info: SOA is a design philosophy, not a technology; it doesn't require web services, and using web services doesn't make it SOA; it isn't new (EDI, CORBA, DCOM); it's a means not an end; build it incrementally; it needs tools, not consultants.

title: Impact of SOA on jobs
info: A clearer split between software engineers (application builders) and programmers (service developers); shorter cycles; more reliable software; fewer programming-only jobs, more software-engineering jobs.

title: IService.cs
info: In a WCF project, holds the service contract: an interface marked [ServiceContract] whose methods are marked [OperationContract]. Signatures only, no implementation. (For REST it also carries [WebGet].)

title: Service.svc.cs
info: The implementation class: an ordinary class that implements the IService interface and contains the method bodies.

title: Add Service Reference
info: Visual Studio feature that reads a service's WSDL and generates a static client proxy class at design/compile time.

title: Static vs. dynamic binding (SOC)
info: Static: the proxy is created at compile time (Add Service Reference). Dynamic (dynamic proxy): the service is chosen and bound at run time.
example: A travel site reading airline service URLs from a text file at run time.

title: Dynamic binding (OO)
info: A method call is bound to a method's address at run time instead of compile time. Requires a virtual method so a child class can override it.
example: `Animal a = new Dog(); a.Speak();` prints "Woof".

title: InstanceContextMode (WCF)
info: PerCall: a new service object per call. PerSession: one object per client session. Single: one shared object for everyone.
example: PerCall calculator; PerSession shopping cart; Single site-wide hit counter.

title: ConcurrencyMode (WCF)
info: Single: one thread at a time per instance. Reentrant: single, but allows callbacks to re-enter. Multiple: many threads at once, so you must synchronize.

title: Program vs. process/thread
info: A program (method) is static code. A process or thread is that code while running, together with its state and resources. A service is a class being hosted and executed.

title: Time slicing
info: On one processor, threads only appear to run in parallel because the CPU switches between them. True parallelism needs multiple cores or processors.

title: Thread stack vs. shared data
info: Each thread has its own stack for local variables. Shared data (static fields, shared objects) is visible to all threads and needs synchronization.

title: Heap vs. stack vs. static memory
info: Code and static data have sizes known at compile time. Objects created with `new` live on the heap. Local value-type variables live on the stack.

title: fork()
info: Unix call that copies the parent process. Returns 0 in the child, the child's PID in the parent, and −1 on error (only cause: out of resources).

title: exec (execl, execvp)
info: Replaces the current process image with a new program. Returns only if there's an error.

title: wait() (Unix)
info: The parent process blocks until a child process terminates. A shell waits for foreground commands but not background ones (`&`).

title: SimShell
info: The case-study command interpreter built on fork + execvp + wait, with foreground and background execution.

title: Critical operation
info: An operation on a shared resource that gives wrong results if it is interleaved or interrupted halfway.
example: Two ATM withdrawals both reading a $1,000 balance before either writes.

title: Race condition (lost update)
info: The result depends on thread timing. Two threads read the same value, both modify it, and one write overwrites the other.
example: Two simultaneous likes on a 41-like post leave it at 42.

title: Deadlock
info: Each party holds a resource while waiting for one another holds, so none can ever proceed.
example: Transfer A→B locks A then waits for B; transfer B→A locks B then waits for A.

title: Deadlock prevention
info: Design the system so the deadlock condition can never arise.
example: Always lock the lower-numbered account first.

title: Deadlock avoidance
info: Predict that a deadlock is likely and refuse or delay the request.
example: Traffic lights; level-crossing gates.

title: Deadlock detection and recovery
info: Let deadlocks happen, detect them, then force a thread to release what it holds.
example: A database picks a "deadlock victim" and rolls it back.

title: Livelock
info: Threads keep changing state in response to each other; resources stay free (unlike deadlock), but no one makes progress.
example: Two people sidestepping each other in a hallway.

title: Binary exponential backoff
info: Ethernet's (CSMA/CD) livelock fix: after the n-th collision, wait a random 0 to 2ⁿ−1 time slots.
example: After the 4th collision: 0–15 slots.

title: Starvation
info: A thread could get the resource in principle but never does in practice, often because higher-priority threads keep winning.

title: Aging
info: Starvation fix: raise a thread's priority the longer it waits.

title: Two ways to create a Java thread
info: (A) Extend Thread and override run(). (B) Implement Runnable and pass it to `new Thread(r)`. Use B when your class already extends another class (single inheritance).

title: start() vs. run() (Java)
info: start() creates a new thread that calls run(). Calling run() directly just runs the method on the current thread; no new thread is created.

title: Java thread priorities
info: Range 1–10: MIN_PRIORITY 1, NORM_PRIORITY 5 (default), MAX_PRIORITY 10. Equal priorities run round-robin; higher preempts lower.

title: Thread life cycle
info: Created → (start) ready → (dispatch) running → back to ready when the time slice ends. From running: waiting (wait/notify), sleeping (sleep), blocked, or terminated.

title: Busy waiting (spinning)
info: Looping on a condition such as `while(!writeable){}`. Wastes CPU time, and without a lock the check-then-set can still be interrupted.

title: Intrinsic lock (Java monitor)
info: Every Java object has a lock. A synchronized method or block acquires it; other synchronized access to that object blocks until it's released.

title: wait() / notify() / notifyAll() (Java)
info: wait() releases the object's lock and puts the thread in the waiting state. notify() wakes one waiting thread; notifyAll() wakes all. Called only while holding the lock.

title: Synchronized method facts
info: Locks the object for the whole method (can cause unnecessary blocking or deadlock); unsynchronized methods can still access the object; reentrant (a thread can re-acquire its own lock); the thread can still be interrupted inside it.

title: Synchronized statement (block)
info: `synchronized(obj){...}` locks only obj, only for the block: finer-grained than a synchronized method.

title: Protecting a static field
info: `synchronized(this)` only locks one instance, so different instances can still update a static field at once. Lock on the class instead, e.g. `synchronized(Order.class)`.

title: join()
info: Blocks the calling thread until the target thread finishes. Without it, main may exit first, killing child threads and the shared objects it created.

title: C# vs. C++ basics
info: In C#, Main is a static method in a class; no global variables; single class inheritance but many interfaces; `override` keyword required; garbage collected; switch has no fall-through; pointers only in unsafe code; `==` compares string contents.

title: Boxing / unboxing
info: Boxing wraps a value type in a reference type: `object x = v;`. Unboxing casts it back: `int v2 = (int)x;`.

title: C# numeric sizes
info: byte 8 bits (0–255), int 32, long 64 (always), float 32 (~7 digits), double 64 (~16 digits), decimal 128 (~28 digits, literal `3.0m`), char 16 (Unicode).

title: Python threading.Thread
info: `t = threading.Thread(target=func, args=("P1",))`, then `t.start()` and `t.join()`. Without join, the main thread can finish before its children.

title: Python global declaration
info: A function must declare `global x` to modify a shared module-level variable.

title: threading.Lock / threading.Condition
info: Lock gives mutual exclusion (`acquire()`, `release()` in finally). Condition replaces polling: `with cv:` then `cv.wait()` / `cv.notify()`.

title: System.Threading namespace
info: Thread, Monitor, ReaderWriterLock, Mutex, Semaphore, AutoResetEvent, ManualResetEvent, Interlocked.

title: Thread methods (C#)
info: Start, Join, Sleep, Abort, Interrupt, Suspend, Resume.

title: Thread properties (C#)
info: CurrentThread, IsAlive, IsBackground, Name, Priority (Highest, AboveNormal, Normal, BelowNormal, Lowest), ThreadState.

title: Foreground vs. background thread
info: Threads are foreground by default and keep the process alive until they finish. Background threads (IsBackground = true) are killed when the last foreground thread ends.

title: ThreadStart vs. ParameterizedThreadStart
info: ThreadStart delegates a method with no parameters: `new Thread(new ThreadStart(obj.Run))`. ParameterizedThreadStart takes one `object` argument, passed in `Start(arg)`.

title: Monitor.Enter / Monitor.Exit
info: Acquire and release an object's lock in C#. Enter blocks until the lock is free. Put Exit in a `finally` block so the lock is never orphaned.

title: lock statement (C#)
info: `lock(obj){...}` is shorthand for Monitor.Enter(obj); try {...} finally { Monitor.Exit(obj); }. C#'s equivalent of Java's synchronized block. C# has no synchronized methods.

title: Orphaned lock
info: A lock that is never released because the thread threw an exception or exited before Exit. Prevented by calling Exit in a finally block.

title: Monitor.TryEnter
info: Tries to acquire the lock, optionally with a timeout (ms or TimeSpan) and a `ref bool lockTaken`. Gives up instead of blocking forever.
example: An autosave that skips this round if the file is busy for more than 100 ms.

title: Monitor.Wait / Pulse / PulseAll
info: C#'s versions of Java's wait / notify / notifyAll. Wait releases the lock and waits; Pulse wakes one waiting thread; PulseAll wakes all. Must hold the lock to call them.

title: Why `while`, not `if`, around Wait
info: After waking, the condition may no longer be true (another thread got there first), so re-check it in a loop.

title: Producer/consumer (shared buffer)
info: Producers write to and consumers read from a shared buffer. They communicate through the buffer cell (data) and a flag such as `writeable`; both set and get must be synchronized.
example: A restaurant ticket rail between waiters and cooks.

title: ReaderWriterLock
info: Allows read/read overlap but not read/write or write/write. You must create an instance; AcquireReaderLock / AcquireWriterLock take timeouts. It doesn't name an object; it protects whatever code is between acquire and release.

title: SyncBlock
info: How Monitor is implemented: each object header holds a SyncBlock index pointing into a SyncBlock table that stores the lock.

title: Mutex
info: WaitOne() / ReleaseMutex(). Can synchronize across processes (named mutex); the OS frees it if the owner dies. Orders of magnitude slower than Monitor.
example: Allowing only one copy of an app to run.

title: Named mutex / semaphore risk
info: Named sync objects are system-wide, so malicious code can create one with the same name and interfere (denial of service).

title: Indivisible (atomic) instruction
info: A hardware instruction that tests and sets one bit or word in a single uninterruptible step. Used to build locks and semaphores ("who locks the lock?").

title: Test-and-set / LL-SC
info: Hardware support for atomicity: MC68000 BSET, BCLR, BCHG; MIPS Load Linked / Store Conditional (SC fails if the location changed after LL).

title: Atomic instruction vs. object lock
info: Use an atomic instruction when the critical operation is a single update of one word or bit (e.g. `Interlocked.Increment`). Use an object lock when a sequence of statements must run as a unit.

title: Semaphore (concept)
info: A non-negative integer s that limits users of a pool of R identical resources to R or fewer. wait(s): if s > 0, s−−, else block. signal(s): s++. Both are indivisible.
example: A parking garage's "spaces free" sign.

title: C# Semaphore(initial, max)
info: WaitOne() decrements and blocks at 0. Release() increments and returns the previous count. Releasing past the max throws SemaphoreFullException.

title: Semaphore + lock together
info: A semaphore counts resources but isn't tied to the objects, so two threads can still pick the same cell. Pair it with a lock on the cells.

title: Locks vs. coordination events
info: Locks/monitors guard a resource while threads compete; who wins doesn't matter (tennis). Coordination events set the order threads run in (table tennis). Also called thread triggers.

title: AutoResetEvent
info: Each Set() releases exactly one waiting thread, then the event resets itself automatically.
example: A subway turnstile.

title: ManualResetEvent
info: Set() releases all waiting threads, and the event stays set until you call Reset().
example: A stadium gate.

title: Polling vs. event-driven
info: Polling (control flow) repeatedly checks for a change; fine for slow sensors. Event-driven: the source notifies subscribers when something happens.
example: Refreshing email every 30 s vs. a push notification.

title: Delegate
info: A type that refers to methods with a particular signature, like a C++ function pointer. Lets you pass a method as a parameter.

title: Multicast delegate
info: A delegate holding several methods; invoking it calls each in the order added. This is how an event notifies every subscriber.

title: Defining an event (two parts)
info: A subscription container (an `event` of a delegate type) and an emitter method that raises the event when there are subscribers.

title: Subscribing to an event
info: `+=` subscribes a handler and `-=` unsubscribes it. Check for null (no subscribers) before raising.
example: `Hotel.PriceCut += new PriceCutEvent(agency.RoomOnSale);`

title: Callback / event handler
info: The subscriber's method that the event source calls when the event fires.

title: ref vs. out
info: `ref` passes by reference and must be initialized before the call. `out` is output-only and needn't be initialized first.

title: Hotel/Agency case study
info: Hotels raise a priceCut event when a new price is lower than the current one; subscribed agencies' roomOnSale handlers run. One hotel thread and N agency threads, started by Main.

title: Which thread runs an event handler?
info: The thread that raised the event. In the Hotel example roomOnSale runs on the hotel thread, so Thread.CurrentThread.Name there is not the agency's name.

title: Synchronous call
info: The caller blocks and waits for the response.
example: Standing at the counter until your food is ready.

title: Asynchronous one-way call
info: The caller sends and continues; there is no response.
example: Dropping a comment card in a box.

title: Asynchronous callback
info: The caller continues; the callee later calls back into a handler with the result.
example: The restaurant texts you when your order is ready.

title: Async non-blocking with a waiter thread
info: The caller continues while a separate thread waits for the response.
example: Sending a friend to wait at the counter.

title: Task / async / await
info: Task (System.Threading.Tasks) runs work on the thread pool. An async method returns Task<T>. `await` suspends the method and frees the processor until the task finishes. No callback needed.

title: Busy-wait jobTime vs. Task.Delay
info: jobTime(ms) spins and holds the processor. `await Task.Delay(ms)` waits without using the processor.

title: Sync vs. async total time
info: Synchronous total = the sum of the calls. Asynchronous total = the longest parallel call plus any synchronous part.

title: Levels of multithreading support
info: Single thread (serial) → multithreading on one core (context switching) → hyperthreading → multi-core (true parallelism).

title: Hyperthreading
info: Duplicates the control unit, registers and interrupt logic but shares execution units, so the OS sees two logical processors per core.
example: "Cores: 8, Logical processors: 16".

title: Intel TBB
info: Threading Building Blocks, a C++ library that turns synchronous blocking calls into async non-blocking (event-driven) ones and flattens nested calls.

title: Promise
info: An object the caller gets from an async request and can wait on later. Succeeds only if all its tasks succeed; fails if any fails. JavaScript Promise.all; C# Task.

title: OpenMP / Pthreads
info: OpenMP: compiler directives for parallelism in C, C++ and Fortran. Pthreads: the POSIX threads library.

title: Speedup
info: S = T(1 thread) / T(N threads).
example: 120 s on 1 core, 20 s on 8 cores → S = 6.

title: Efficiency
info: E = S / N, where N is the number of threads or cores.
example: S = 6 on 8 cores → E = 75%.

title: Why speedup < N (or < 1)
info: Creating and coordinating threads has overhead. Bigger problems use threads more efficiently; more threads lower efficiency; with enough overhead the parallel version is slower than serial (S < 1).

title: Collatz (HOTPO) problem
info: If n is even, n → n/2; if odd, n → 3n+1. Conjecture: every start reaches 1.

title: Collatz case-study lessons
info: Contiguous blocks gave the last thread the biggest numbers (slowest thread decides total time); modulo split balanced the load but showed >100% efficiency because the single-thread baseline used one huge array. Lesson: compare fair implementations.

title: Partial correctness vs. termination
info: Partial correctness: output is right whenever the program terminates (proved by induction or symbolic execution). Termination: it always halts, e.g. a loop variable strictly decreases.

title: WCF
info: Windows Communication Foundation: supports platform-independent and platform-specific services, distributed transactions and WS-* specifications.

title: targetNamespace / xmlns prefixes
info: In WSDL, targetNamespace names the namespace being defined; prefixes like tns, xsd1 and soap qualify element and type names.

title: WSDL types and message elements
info: types defines data types (like a C typedef); message elements declare an operation's inputs and outputs using those types.
example: StockQuote: GetLastTradePrice takes a string tickerSymbol, returns a float price.

title: HTTP request line
info: Method SP Request-URI SP HTTP-Version CRLF. Method names are case-sensitive.
example: `GET /books/42 HTTP/1.1`

title: HTTP status line
info: HTTP-Version SP Status-Code SP Reason-Phrase CRLF.
example: `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`, `404 Not Found`, `500 Internal Server Error`.

title: GET
info: Retrieves the resource identified by the URI (or the data a process at that URI produces).

title: HEAD
info: Same as GET, but the server must not return a body. Used for metadata, e.g. checking existence or size.

title: PUT
info: Creates or replaces the resource at the given URI.

title: POST
info: Adds the enclosed entity as a new subordinate of the resource (appends); the server picks its location.
example: POST /books adds a book and the server assigns id 43.

title: DELETE
info: Deletes the resource. Success isn't guaranteed even with a success status (the server may only move it).

title: TRACE / CONNECT
info: TRACE: loop-back test of the request. CONNECT: for a proxy that switches to a tunnel, e.g. SSL.

title: POST vs. PUT
info: POST: "here's something new, you decide where it goes" (append). PUT: "put this exactly at this address" (replace or create there).

title: REST
info: Representational State Transfer. Stateless communication that transfers representations of resources, each identified by a URI, over HTTP's uniform interface.

title: Roy Fielding
info: Defined REST in his 2000 PhD dissertation; a principal author of HTTP 1.0 and 1.1.

title: REST constraint: client-server
info: Clients and servers are separate and talk through a uniform HTTP interface.

title: REST constraint: stateless
info: Each request is treated as if it came from a new client; every request carries everything needed.
example: Every API call includes your auth token.

title: REST constraint: cacheable
info: Responses contain what's needed to reuse them on the client side.

title: REST constraint: layered
info: Requests can be redirected transparently through intermediaries, even several times.
example: A CDN in front of a site.

title: REST constraint: code on demand
info: The server can execute code itself or send a script to run on the client.
example: JavaScript sent with a web page.

title: SOAP vs. REST
info: SOAP focuses on the verb (call a remote method), is class-based and heavyweight, best for computation. REST focuses on the noun (access a resource), is lightweight and script-callable, best for data and resources.

title: Converting a WCF SOAP service to REST
info: (1) `using System.ServiceModel.Web;` in IService.cs; (2) add [WebGet] (with UriTemplate for 2+ args); (3) add `Factory="System.ServiceModel.Activation.WebServiceHostFactory"` to the .svc markup; (4) remove <system.serviceModel> from Web.config. Service.svc.cs doesn't change.

title: [WebGet] and UriTemplate
info: [WebGet] exposes an operation over HTTP GET. UriTemplate maps URL parts to parameters; needed for 2+ arguments.
example: `[WebGet(UriTemplate = "add2?x={x}&y={y}")]`

title: Calling REST with WebClient
info: Build the URL (base + operation + parameters, e.g. with UriTemplate.BindByPosition), then `new WebClient().DownloadString(uri)`; or DownloadData + MemoryStream + DataContractSerializer.

title: Calling REST with HttpClient
info: Asynchronous: `client.GetAsync("").Result`, then `response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync().Result`.

title: Parts of a REST URL
info: Base URL, operation, then `?` and the parameters separated by `&`.
example: `.../weather/forecast?zip=85281&days=3`

title: ASP.NET Web API
info: RESTful services without WCF, installed via NuGet (Microsoft.AspNet.WebApi). MVC-style, with Configuration and Controllers folders.

title: Web API route template
info: `config.Routes.MapHttpRoute("DefaultApi", "api/{controller}/{id}", ...)` with id optional; plus `config.MapHttpAttributeRoutes()`. Registered from Global.asax's Application_Start.
example: GET /api/products/5 → ProductsController.Get(5).

title: ApiController
info: Base class for Web API controllers. The HTTP method picks the C# method.
example: `HelloController : ApiController { public string Get() ... }` at /api/hello.

title: Hosting options
info: IIS Express/localhost for development; an IIS server or the cloud for professional hosting; self-hosting (running the service as threads in your own app) for low volume.

title: http.sys
info: IIS's kernel-mode listener. Receives requests from browsers and queues them (Reactor pattern). Isolated from crashes in user code.

title: Web Administration Service (WAS)
info: Handles configuration: registers web services and applications in the registry/metabase, and adds them to an existing request queue or creates a new one.

title: IIS worker process (w3wp.exe)
info: User-mode process that executes web services and applications as its threads.

title: Just-In-Time (JIT) deployment
info: Source is deployed and compiled on the first request, so the first request is slower; source can be redeployed while the service is being accessed. (Pre-compiled requires recompiling and redeploying the project.)

title: Ideal service broker
info: Publishes requirements and GUI templates, registers and tests services, keeps a QoS database, and helps builders assemble applications.

title: UDDI
info: Universal Description, Discovery and Integration: a registry standard started by Microsoft, IBM and Ariba in 2000. Five data structures, each defined in XML Schema.

title: businessEntity
info: UDDI white pages. The provider: UUID businessKey, name, description, contacts, list of services, identifiers (DUNS) and categories (NAICS).

title: businessService
info: UDDI yellow pages. One service: serviceKey and businessKey, name, description, its bindingTemplates and categories.

title: bindingTemplate
info: UDDI green pages. The technical description that links a businessService to an actual implementation: accessPoint (URL) and tModelInstanceDetails. One service can have several.

title: tModel
info: A technical model or specification, such as a WSDL interface type. A service declares that it implements one by referencing its tModelKey.

title: publisherAssertion
info: A relationship between two businessEntities (fromKey, toKey, keyedReference). Visible only when both parties publish it, so no one can falsely claim a relationship.

title: UDDI inquiry API
info: find_business, find_service, find_binding, find_tModel, the get_*Detail calls, and get_registeredInfo.

title: UDDI publishing and security APIs
info: Publishing: save_* and delete_*. Security: get_authToken and discard_authToken.

title: find_business arguments
info: maxRows, findQualifiers (e.g. exactNameMatch), name (up to 5 in UDDI 2.0), discoveryURLs, identifierBag, categoryBag, tModelBag.

title: XML Schema
info: Defines the structure of an XML tree, the way a database schema defines tables.

title: Ontology (vs. database)
info: Captures meaning and relationships between concepts, allowing semantic search and reasoning.
example: Finds "vehicle hire" when you search "car rental".

title: HTTP is stateless
info: Each request looks like it's from a new client, and ASP.NET builds a fresh page object per request, so class fields don't survive between requests.

title: ViewState
info: Stores values in a hidden field of the generated page via `ViewState["name"]`. Survives postbacks but is readable from the current page only.

title: Cross-page posting
info: Transfers data to another page: post back to the server with `PostBackUrl="Dest.aspx"`, then the destination page calls a public method on the source page.

title: Session state
info: Server memory, per user session.
example: A shopping cart while you browse.

title: Application state
info: Server memory shared by all sessions.
example: A "142 people viewing now" counter.

title: Cookies
info: State stored on the client's computer, so it survives closing the browser.
example: "Remember me for 30 days".

title: Text/XML file state
info: Data written to a file in the server's App_Data folder survives server restarts. Uses Path.Combine(HttpRuntime.AppDomainAppPath, "App_Data"), StreamWriter/StreamReader, File.Exists.

title: File upload (ASP.NET)
info: Check FileUploadControl.HasFile, get the folder with Server.MapPath("~/"), create it if missing, then SaveAs(path + filename), inside try/catch.

title: Dynamic proxy
info: Binds a service at run time: find and analyze the WSDL for operations and types, then create the proxy (e.g. DynamicProxyFactory → CreateProxy → CallMethod). Used for services not bound at compile time.

title: Web service testing tool
info: Black-box testing from only a WSDL: analyze it for URL, operations and types, generate test cases from input types, invoke dynamically (dynamic proxy), analyze results.

title: Binding to a RESTful service
info: Always dynamic: the client builds base URL + operation + parameters at run time. With no WSDL, programs can't discover operations automatically, so automated testing is harder.

title: Nonremotable object
info: Can't leave its application domain. Most .NET base classes are nonremotable.

title: Marshal-by-reference
info: The object stays put; the client gets a proxy that forwards calls. The web-services model.
example: Sharing a Google Docs link.

title: Marshal-by-value
info: The object is copied to the other application domain (migration / code integration).
example: Emailing a .docx attachment.

title: Why web services use only marshal-by-reference
info: Marshal-by-value requires the same language environment on both sides, which breaks platform independence.

title: Remoting vs. web services (protocol)
info: Remoting and remote APIs use TCP (connection-oriented). Web services and Web APIs use HTTP (message-oriented). Remote APIs suit embedded/IoT devices without HTTP.

title: .NET Remoting server and client
info: Server class extends MarshalByRefObject. Client: new TcpClientChannel → ChannelServices.RegisterChannel → RemotingConfiguration.RegisterWellKnownClientType(type, "tcp://...") → `new SvrClock()` returns a proxy.

title: Java RMI
info: Remote Method Invocation for distributed Java apps. Uses marshal-by-reference; the remote object extends UnicastRemoteObject, is registered in a directory (LDAP in the example, via bind/lookup), and the client calls it through a stub.

title: AJAX
info: Asynchronous JavaScript and XML. Runs in the browser and refreshes part of a page without reloading it, making pages more responsive.
example: Google search suggestions; Gmail showing new mail.

title: XMLHttpRequest flow
info: Create the XMLHttpRequest (ActiveXObject in old IE), set `onreadystatechange`, call `open('GET', url, true)` (true = async) and `send(null)`; the callback uses responseText.

title: AJAX success check
info: `readyState == 4 && status == 200`: request done and HTTP OK.

title: AJAX drawbacks
info: Complex client-side JavaScript; single-page model with no page transitions; not supported by every browser.

title: ASP.NET AJAX (server-side AJAX)
info: Formerly "Atlas". Mark the refreshable part of a page with a ScriptManager plus an UpdatePanel instead of writing JavaScript.
